Part 3 – Six Action Tracks: Each track has specific high-level actions and deliverables (e.g., Action 1.1: Legal and workforce capacity; Action 6.1: Ecosystem protection)

Part 4 – Governance and M&E: Clear roles for the Quadripartite Secretariat, OHHLEP, and regional coordination platforms; monitoring aligned with SDG contributions and national workplan

Part 5 – Resource Mobilization: Joint strategy for sustainable financing, targeting trust funds and donor alignment for LMIC implementation support

instrument: MRLs and Risk Management Recommendations for Residues of Veterinary Drugs in Foods (CXM 2-2023)
description: Compendium of standards for chemical residues in food from veterinary drugs. It lists the maximum residue limits (MRLs) – the highest levels of specific veterinary drug residues permitted in foods (meat, milk, eggs, etc.) – that are considered safe for consumers, based on scientific risk assessments. It also includes risk management recommendations (RMRs) for certain drugs (e.g. when no safe level can be determined). Helps countries regulate veterinary drug use and ensure that animal-derived foods are chemically safe for human consumption.
governanceRole:
Harmonized international benchmark: encourages regulatory cooperation. Food safety authorities and veterinary drug regulators must work together – the former rely on the standard to set national residue limits and testing programs, while the latter control drug use on farms to meet those limits.
Surveillance and testing: Coordination (often through national residue control plans) is a One Health governance success, requiring joint surveillance, data sharing, and cross-agency enforcement. The Codex MRL list, developed with global scientific input (JECFA evaluations), helps countries align their policies, thus smoothing trade and encouraging all countries to build capacity for residue monitoring and laboratory testing.
limitations:
Capacity and regulatory: Countries with limited laboratory or monitoring capacity may struggle to enforce MRLs, leading to gaps in consumer protection and animal drug oversight. Another challenge is ensuring veterinary and food safety authorities coordinate effectively – if veterinary services do not enforce prudent use or if farmers are unaware of withdrawal requirements, residues can still end up in food above the limits.
Focus on consumers: focuses on consumer health; it does not directly address environmental residues or occupational exposure, which means additional measures (outside Codex) are needed to fully protect ecosystems and farm workers.
Finite list: Codex MRLs exist for a finite list of drugs – national authorities must manage risks from veterinary chemicals not yet evaluated by Codex, which can complicate a unified One Health strategy.
provisions:
Section 2: Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) – Defines limits for veterinary drug residues in food to ensure consumer safety.

Annex: Risk Management Recommendations – Lists drugs prohibited in food-producing animals due to human health risks.
interlinkages: WTO SPS Agreement

instrument: Decision 16/19: Global Action Plan for Biodiversity and Health
description: Adopts the Global Action Plan on Biodiversity and Health, supporting the implementation of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It recognizes biodiversity as a determinant of health, supports One Health among other multisectoral approaches, and outlines voluntary actions for Parties to integrate biodiversity–health interlinkages into national strategies, with a focus on equity and multisectoral governance.
governanceRole:
Operationalizes biodiversity-health linkages across 8 GBF targets: The Action Plan provides clear guidance on how to embed One Health into land use, species management, pollution control, and AMR governance (Annex §§13)
Formalizes One Health governance structures: Calls for national focal points, interministerial coordination, and cross-sector assessment tools (Annex §§12d, 12g, 12j)
Promotes inclusive implementation: Includes gender, Indigenous peoples, youth, and persons with disabilities in policy design and monitoring (Annex §§12e, 12f).
limitations:
Resource and capacity gaps not fully mitigated: While funding is encouraged, no earmarked mechanisms exist under this decision (Decision §7, Annex §4)
Limited integration with public health system mandates: While the Action Plan bridges sectors, few specific mandates are assigned to ensure reporting (Decision §§6–9)
provisions:
Decision §1: Adopts the Global Action Plan on Biodiversity and Health as a voluntary tool aligned with the GBF.

Decision §3(a–d): Encourages national implementation, coordination, focal point designation, youth participation, and policy mainstreaming.

Annex §12: Lists general actions for biodiversity–health integration across governance, policy, education, surveillance, and inclusive participation.

Annex §13: Aligns One Health implementation actions with GBF Targets 1–8, across land use, species management, invasive species, pollution, and climate
interlinkages:
Convention on Biological Diversity
Kunming-Montreal GBF

instrument: Provisional Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Sustainable Management of Plastics in Agriculture
description: Provides guiding principles and measures that governments, manufacturers, and other agrifood system stakeholders may adopt to promote sustainable management practices for plastics used in agriculture. It covers all agricultural sub-sectors, including crops, livestock, fisheries, aquaculture, and forestry, and addresses the full lifecycle of plastics from design and manufacture through to end-of-life management. The Code is organized around seven interconnected goals, including contributing to food security, reducing plastic use that poses risks to the environment or human health, promoting sustainable product design, eliminating leakage into the environment, and supporting equitable participation of affected populations, including smallholder farmers, women, youth, and Indigenous Peoples.
governanceRole:
Establishes a cross-sectoral policy framework linking agricultural plastic management to human, animal, and environmental health. Objectives explicitly include protecting human and animal health, food safety, soil, and water from agricultural plastic pollution, providing a governance basis for addressing a diffuse, multi-pathway environmental health risk.
Promotes evidence-building and monitoring to guide decision-making: Countries are encouraged to develop strategies to measure and monitor plastics use and alternatives, and to cooperate on common data collection and reporting approaches, including relevant SDG indicators.
Supports national policy development and technical cooperation: FAO commits to developing specific technical guidelines and manuals to support implementation, and encourages countries to build their own regulatory frameworks with particular support to developing countries, economies in transition, and Small Island Developing States.
limitations:
Relationship to a future legally binding instrument: The VCoC was developed in parallel with negotiations for an international legally binding instrument on plastic pollution (INC process); it is intended to complement, not preempt, that process, and its scope and status may evolve depending on the outcome of those negotiations.
Non-binding monitoring: Countries are invited to monitor implementation and report to FAO on a voluntary basis only, with no formal compliance or review mechanism established.
provisions:
Article 2.1(ii) – Objectives: States that the VCoC aims to protect human and animal health, food safety, food security, soil, water, and the environment from pollution resulting from the use of plastics in agriculture.

Article 4.6.1(iv) – Research and Development: Calls on stakeholders to examine the pathways and impacts of plastics used in agriculture, including microplastics, on agroecosystems, food safety, and human health.

Article 5.2.2 – Alternatives Assessment: Requires that alternative practices and products be assessed for their potential impact on human, animal, and soil health, agrifood systems, and the environment, considering unintended consequences and trade-offs.
interlinkages:
Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal
International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management

instrument: WOAH One Health Strategy
description: Roadmap for embedding One Health within veterinary services, this strategy highlights multisectoral coordination, workforce capacity, and investment needed to manage zoonoses, AMR, food safety, and environmental health—aligned with the Quadripartite One Health Joint Plan of Action. It emphasizes veterinary leadership, national operational tools (e.g., MCM OT), and workforce development as vehicles for holistic health resilience.
governanceRole:
Positions veterinary services as One Health change-agents: It calls for operationalizing coordination mechanisms (e.g., MCM OT) to link veterinary, human and environmental health governance
Focuses on workforce competency: The strategy advances competency-based training, mentorship, and certification for field epidemiologists and veterinary personnel working at spillover hotspots
Promotes integrated surveillance and data systems: WOAH supports WAHIS and WAHIS-Wild for real-time reporting and cross-sector risk communication and climate-informed surveillance
limitations:
Environment sector engagement remains secondary: While environmental data is referenced, formal partnership with environmental agencies across member countries is inconsistent
Resource constraints hinder implementation: The roadmap depends on investment and capacity that many low- and middle-income countries may struggle to mobilize without external support
Strategy is not enforceable: The strategy's impact relies on alignment with national policy priorities and sustained funding
provisions:
Governance Pillar: Endorses use of the Multisectoral Coordination Mechanisms Operational Tool (MCM OT) to create national One Health coordinating bodies

Workforce Development Pillar: Mandates competency-based training systems for field epidemiology, continuing education, and mentorship across zoonotic and environmental health domains

Surveillance & Information Sharing Pillar: Supports the use of WAHIS and WAHIS-Wild for joint veterinary–environmental disease monitoring and early warning systems
interlinkages:
One Health Joint Plan of Action
International Health Regulations (IHR)

instrument: Global Action Plan on Climate Change and Health (A78/27)
description: Adopted by WHA decision WHA78(27). A framework aligning health and climate action. It integrates health into climate policies through three areas: leadership and advocacy, evidence and monitoring, and country-level capacity-building. The plan promotes equity, One Health and planetary health approaches, and multisectoral collaboration to strengthen climate-resilient, low-carbon health systems and reduce climate-related health risks.
governanceRole:
Equity (pp. 1, 4, 10): Prioritizes vulnerable populations, equity in climate–health financing, and locally led strategies.
One Health integration (p. 10): Promotes intersectoral cooperation linking human, animal, and environmental health in national strategies.
Evidence and monitoring (pp. 7–9): Strengthens research, surveillance, and integrated data systems on climate-sensitive diseases.
Capacity building (pp. 4, 11–14): Provides technical guidance and tools for climate-resilient, low-carbon health systems.
limitations:
Resource dependence (pp. 4, 13): Implementation relies on mobilizing external funding, creating disparities for low-income countries.
Coordination complexity (p. 15): Broad multisectoral scope may slow progress due to need for extensive alignment among actors.
Uneven national uptake (p. 10): Actions are nationally determined, risking uneven implementation and impact.
provisions:
Action Area – Leadership, Coordination and Advocacy: Calls on countries to integrate health into national climate plans, mobilize financing, and ensure the health sector participates in climate policy, while WHO coordinates global advocacy and technical support.

Action Area – Evidence and Monitoring: Strengthens research, data, and surveillance on climate-sensitive diseases, and establishes systems to track climate–health risks and the benefits of mitigation and adaptation.

Action Area – Country-Level Action and Capacity-Building: Promotes national strategies for climate-resilient, low-carbon health systems, periodic vulnerability assessments, and support for adaptation planning and finance.
interlinkages:
UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
Paris Agreement
WHA 72(9) Global Strategy on Health, Environment & Climate Change

instrument: Global strategy for the prevention and control of high pathogenic avian influenza (2024–2033)
description: Provides a ten-year roadmap to reduce the impacts of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI), especially the H5Nx 2.3.4.4b clade, through a One Health systems approach. It focuses on prevention, protection, and transformation of poultry value chains to mitigate disease, safeguard wildlife and human health, and promote sustainable agrifood systems. The strategy emphasizes risk-based surveillance, integrated animal-wildlife-human data systems, vaccination stewardship, inclusive governance, and sustainable biosecurity. It seeks to build resilient poultry systems while addressing the pandemic potential and ecological disruption caused by HPAI.
governanceRole:
Anchors One Health within operational animal disease control: The strategy embeds One Health into concrete surveillance, vaccination, and biosecurity programs, particularly at the poultry–wildlife–human interface, creating tangible cross-sector pathways for risk reduction​
Strengthens integrated surveillance and response systems: It promotes joint risk-based surveillance across domestic and wild species, facilitates laboratory cooperation, and supports cross-sectoral data sharing through OFFLU and national platforms
Builds institutional capacity through multi-level governance: The strategy establishes global and regional steering committees, intersectoral task forces, and public–private collaboration mechanisms that integrate veterinary, public health, and environmental institutions
limitations:
National-level buy-in and funding are uneven: The strategy assumes countries will prioritize HPAI and invest in One Health capacity, but many LMICs lack dedicated budgets or multisectoral structures, creating gaps in operational delivery and equity
Limited operational inclusion of public health authorities: Despite strong global-level engagement from WHO and public health actors, the strategy offers few mechanisms to systematically embed human health agencies at the country level, especially outside of outbreak response
provisions:
Objective 1, pg. 5: Using a One Health approach to prevent, detect early and rapidly respond is key to reducing the devastating impacts of HPAI outbreaks in domestic and wild animals, and to preventing virus spillover/spillback to wild animals and humans.

Output 3.1, pg. 11: The strategy supports transformation of poultry agrifood systems... using participatory processes involving poultry producers, wildlife ecologists, public health, and consumer groups to promote safe, resilient, and sustainable production aligned with One Health goals.

Output 1.1, pg. 7: Integrated One Health approaches for risk-based surveillance, prevention and response are required to address threats... Surveillance of diseases in wildlife should be integrated into wildlife management and conservation systems.
interlinkages:
International Health Regulations
PIP Framework
Terrestrial Animal Health Code
